items.title: The Agent Loop
items.description: Build an agent loop that plans, calls tools and stops: step budgets, termination conditions and error handling for LLM agents in Python.
items.use_when: The number of steps is unknown at design time, the next action depends on what the last one returned, and the task has an end state you can recognise — "find the bug in this repo", "get this ticket to done".
items.not_for: A sequence of steps that is fixed and known in advance. That is a chain of calls, and it is cheaper, faster and debuggable. Reaching for a loop because it feels more capable is the most common way to make a simple task expensive and non-deterministic.

items.title: Alembic Schema Migrations
items.description: Alembic migrations done properly: autogenerate review, safe rollbacks, zero-downtime column changes and one ordered history across environments.
items.use_when: More than one person or more than one environment runs the same schema, and you need the change that worked on a laptop to arrive identically in production, in order, with a way back.
items.not_for: A database whose schema is owned by another team or another service. Running migrations against a schema you do not own turns a deploy into a cross-team incident. Also not for data backfills large enough to need batching and resumption — those are jobs with progress and restartability, and hiding one inside a migration means a failed deploy halfway through a rewrite.

items.title: ChromaDB Embedded Vector Store
items.description: ChromaDB as an embedded vector store: persistence, metadata filtering and collection design for prototypes, CLI tools and local retrieval.
items.use_when: You need retrieval working today and infrastructure is the thing in the way — a prototype, a demo, a desktop or CLI tool, a test suite that needs a real vector store, or embedded search inside another product.
items.not_for: A service with several processes writing at once. An embedded store is a library holding a directory, and two writers is not a configuration it has. Also not for a corpus you already know will be large or multi-tenant with hard isolation — starting here then is a migration you have scheduled in advance for no reason.

items.title: Chunking and Embeddings for Retrieval
items.description: Chunking and embedding documents for retrieval: chunk size, overlap, metadata and re-embedding without rebuilding the whole index.
items.use_when: Retrieval quality is the problem and the search itself looks correct — the right index, the right query, and answers built from fragments that do not say enough to answer with.
items.not_for: Documents that are already short and self-contained — a product record, a support macro, a FAQ entry. Splitting those makes them worse. Also not for parsing: extracting clean text from a scanned PDF, a spreadsheet or a slide deck is a separate problem, and this pipeline assumes text that is already correct. Garbage in is chunked faithfully.

items.title: Cursor Pagination
items.description: Cursor pagination for REST APIs: stable ordering, opaque cursors, and paging that does not skip or repeat rows while the list changes.
items.use_when: Paging through a list that changes while a user reads it — feeds, inboxes, activity logs, search results, any admin table — or through a large result set from a script or an export.
items.not_for: A short fixed list you can return whole, or a UI that genuinely needs numbered pages and a total count and can accept a snapshot that drifts.

items.title: Docker Compose for Local Development
items.description: Docker Compose for local development: databases, caches and queues, health checks, seed data and file watching behind one command.
items.use_when: The project needs more than one process to run — an application plus a database, a cache, a queue, an object store — and onboarding currently involves a wiki page with steps that no longer work.
items.not_for: Production orchestration. Compose has no rolling deploys, no health-based traffic shifting and no rescheduling; a stack that runs in it will run, right up until the first node failure. Also not for a single process with no dependencies, where a virtual environment and one command is the whole story.

items.title: Dockerfile for a Production Service
items.description: A production Dockerfile: multi-stage builds, non-root users, small images, correct PID 1 signal handling and reproducible dependency layers.
items.use_when: A service needs an image that ships to a registry and runs somewhere you do not control — a rolling deploy, a scheduler, a colleague's machine — and you want the same bytes to run in all three.
items.not_for: The local development container, which wants the opposite trade-offs: source mounted rather than copied, a reload watcher, dev dependencies present. Building one image that tries to be both produces an image with a compiler in it and a slow inner loop.

items.title: One Error Envelope for an HTTP API
items.description: One error envelope for an HTTP API: stable error codes, machine-readable payloads and handlers that clients and agents can branch on.
items.use_when: Anything with clients — a web app, a mobile app, another service, or an AI agent — needs to react differently to different failures, and you want one shape rather than one per route.
items.not_for: A script or a single-consumer internal tool where a stack trace in the log is the whole requirement.

items.title: LLM Eval Harness
items.description: An LLM eval harness: fixed test sets, deterministic checks, regression gates in CI and scores you can compare between prompt versions.
items.use_when: You are about to make the second change to any system built on a model. The first change you can eyeball; from the second onwards you are trading one set of failures for another and cannot see it.
items.not_for: A prototype nobody depends on yet, and not as a substitute for production monitoring. An offline harness measures a fixed set of inputs; it says nothing about the inputs you have not thought of.

items.title: FastAPI Routers and API Versioning
items.description: FastAPI routers and API versioning: splitting a large main.py into modules, dependency wiring and versioned routes clients can migrate off.
items.use_when: Endpoints are accumulating in one file, or a change to a response shape would break clients you cannot upgrade, or two routes have quietly claimed overlapping paths. Works on an empty application and on one with 800 lines in `main.py` — in the second case the job is to move existing endpoints into modules without changing what any of them does.
items.not_for: A service with a handful of endpoints and one consumer you deploy alongside it. Versioning has a real cost — two code paths, two test suites, a deprecation calendar — and paying it before anyone depends on the old shape buys nothing. Split the file when it hurts; add versions when a client you do not control exists.

items.title: GitHub Actions CD
items.description: GitHub Actions CD: build once and promote the same image, environment approvals, smoke checks after deploy and a rollback you have run.
items.use_when: A service is deployed often enough that doing it by hand is a risk, and CI already runs and blocks merges. This builds on that: it does not repeat the checks, it requires them.
items.not_for: A project with no CI. Automating a deploy that nothing verified means shipping breakage faster and more reliably. Also not for a system where a bad release cannot be undone — a database rewrite, an irreversible external effect — where the correct answer is a manual gate with a human who understands the blast radius.

items.title: GitHub Actions CI
items.description: GitHub Actions CI: pull-request workflows, dependency caching, service containers and required checks that genuinely block a merge.
items.use_when: More than one person merges into a shared branch, or one person merges often enough to have broken it once. Covers the pull-request workflow, dependency caching, service containers, and making the checks actually block a merge.
items.not_for: Deployment. That is a different trust boundary — it needs credentials, environments and approvals, and mixing it into the pull-request workflow is how a fork's pull request gets to run with production access. Also not a substitute for tests: a pipeline running a weak suite tells you the suite is weak, on a schedule.

items.title: Hybrid Search: Keyword + Vector with RRF
items.description: Hybrid search combining keyword and vector retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: two branches, one ranked list, measurable recall gains.
items.use_when: Queries contain identifiers, error codes, SKUs, function names, proper nouns or exact phrases; or recall is short of target with embeddings alone.
items.not_for: A corpus of purely conceptual prose where you have *measured* that lexical search adds nothing. That case is rarer than teams assume — measure the two branches separately before deciding you do not need one.

items.title: Idempotency Keys and Safe Retries
items.description: Idempotency keys and safe retries: making webhooks, payments, queued jobs and client POSTs safe to deliver twice without double effects.
items.use_when: An operation can be delivered or invoked more than once — webhooks, queued jobs, payments, outbound email, any POST a client may retry — and running it twice would double-charge, double-send or double-write.
items.not_for: Naturally idempotent reads, or operations where doing the work twice is genuinely harmless — adding retry machinery to those is cost without benefit.

items.title: JWT Access Token Authentication
items.description: JWT authentication for an API: registration, login, token signing and verification, a current_user dependency, roles and scopes.
items.use_when: An API needs to know who is calling, the callers are your own clients, and you control both sides. Covers registration, login, a `current_user` dependency, roles and scopes.
items.not_for: Long-lived sessions you must be able to revoke, "log out from all devices", or immediately disabling a compromised account. A signed token is valid until it expires and nothing can withdraw it — that needs a server-side session and refresh rotation, which is a separate system with its own threat model. Also not for delegating access to third-party clients: that is OAuth 2, and rolling your own is a bad trade.

items.title: JWT Refresh Tokens and Session Revocation
items.description: JWT refresh tokens and session revocation: rotation, reuse detection, logging out every device and disabling a compromised account.
items.use_when: Users must stay signed in for days or weeks, or you need to end a session on demand — a stolen device, a password change, an administrator disabling an account, a "sign out of all sessions" button.
items.not_for: A service whose clients are machines holding a long-lived key, or an API where a fifteen-minute token is simply reissued from stored credentials. This system exists to hold state about sessions, and if you have nothing to revoke it is cost with no benefit. Half of all projects genuinely do not need it; the other half need all of it.

items.title: LangChain LCEL: Composable Chains
items.description: LangChain LCEL chains: composing prompt, model and parser into one object that streams, batches and falls back, behind a replaceable boundary.
items.use_when: Several places need the same prompt-to-parsed-output path, and you want streaming, batching and fallbacks once rather than per call site.
items.not_for: A single model call in a single place. Wrapping one call in a framework buys an abstraction with no second user and a dependency with its own release schedule. Also not for an agent that decides its own next step — that is a loop with tools, and a linear chain is the wrong shape for it however many branches you add.

items.title: LangChain RAG Retrieval Chain
items.description: A LangChain RAG retrieval chain: retriever, prompt and parser wired for grounded answers, including the follow-up question most chains fail.
items.use_when: Documents are already indexed and searchable, and what is missing is the path from a user's question to a grounded answer — including the second question, which is where most retrieval chains fall over.
items.not_for: Building the index. Chunking, embedding and ingestion decide most of the answer quality and are a separate problem; a retrieval chain over a badly chunked corpus retrieves fragments correctly and answers wrongly. Also not for a corpus small enough to fit in the context window — retrieval there adds a failure mode and removes nothing.

items.title: LangGraph: Agent as a State Graph
items.description: LangGraph agents as state graphs: typed state, reducers, conditional edges, step ceilings and nodes you can test without running the graph.
items.use_when: The next step depends on what the previous step produced — a tool result, a classification, a validation failure — and a fixed sequence of calls cannot express it.
items.not_for: A pipeline whose steps are known before the run starts. That is a composed chain, and a graph adds a state object, a compile step and a checkpoint story for no branching you actually have. Also not for a single model call with one tool, where the provider's own tool loop is smaller than a graph and fails in more obvious ways.

items.title: LangGraph Checkpoints and Human Approval
items.description: LangGraph checkpoints and human approval: durable runs that survive a restart, interrupt-based pauses and idempotent resume semantics.
items.use_when: A run can take longer than the process that started it, or a step in it must not happen until a person says so.
items.not_for: A run that finishes inside one request and does nothing irreversible. Persistence there buys storage cost and a resume path nobody exercises, and an unexercised resume path is worse than none. Also not for approval of *everything* — an approval on every step is an approval on nothing, because it will be clicked through.

items.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
items.description: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation: rubrics, position and verbosity bias, self-preference, and calibration against human labels so a score means something.
items.use_when: You change prompts or models often enough that hand-grading has become the bottleneck, and the quality you care about cannot be checked by an assertion.
items.not_for: Anything a deterministic check can decide. If the answer is valid JSON or not, contains a required field or not, matches a known result or not — assert it. A judge costs money, latency and a calibration programme, and spending all three to check something `==` could have decided is the most common way this goes wrong. Also not for a first prompt with no version to compare against: with nothing to compare, a score is a number with no meaning attached.

items.title: LLM Input Guardrails and Prompt-Injection Detection
items.description: LLM input guardrails and prompt-injection detection: trust boundaries, provenance marking, classifiers and measured false-positive rates.
items.use_when: Model input can contain anything a user typed, or any text fetched from a page, a document, an email or a tool result.
items.not_for: Input the system generated itself from data it already trusts — a templated prompt over your own database rows adds latency and a false-positive rate for an attack surface that is not there. Also not for output-side safety: what the model *produces* is a different check at a different point, and doing both in one function means neither can be tuned.

items.title: Streaming LLM Output in the Browser
items.description: Streaming LLM output in the browser: consuming SSE, incremental rendering, cancellation, reconnects and partial UTF-8 decoding done right.
items.use_when: A backend already streams and the interface has to show it — a chat, a generated document, anything where the user watches text arrive.
items.not_for: A page that renders a completed response. Adding streaming to a client whose server does not stream produces a typewriter animation over an answer that was already whole, which costs complexity and buys the appearance of speed rather than speed. Also not for a client that only needs to know when the work is done — poll a status endpoint.

items.title: Streaming LLM Output over SSE
items.description: Streaming LLM output over SSE from FastAPI: event framing, backpressure, client disconnects, proxy buffering and cancelling the model call.
items.use_when: A model call takes long enough that waiting for the whole answer feels broken — a chat reply, a generated document, a long summary — and the user should see it arrive.
items.not_for: A response the client cannot use until it is complete, such as structured output that has to parse before anything can be done with it. Streaming a JSON object token by token gives the user a progress bar made of syntax and costs you the ability to validate before sending. Also not for two-way traffic: if the client sends messages during generation, that is a WebSocket.

items.title: MCP Client Integration
items.description: MCP client integration: connecting an agent to Model Context Protocol servers, with tool discovery, result budgets, timeouts and failure isolation.
items.use_when: An agent should use tools that somebody else maintains — a hosted service, a colleague's server, a vendor's integration — instead of you writing and keeping a wrapper for each.
items.not_for: Tools you own and deploy alongside the agent. Routing your own function through a protocol and a transport adds a process boundary, a failure mode and a serialisation step to a function call. Also not a substitute for deciding which tools an agent should have: connecting a server with forty tools does not give your agent forty useful tools, it gives it a much harder choice.

items.title: MCP Server over HTTP
items.description: An MCP server over HTTP: authorization, multi-tenancy, rate limits, transport and deployment for agents outside your own organisation.
items.use_when: People outside your organisation should be able to point their agent at your service — a product with an API, an internal platform used by several teams, anything where the caller is not the person who deployed the server.
items.not_for: A server for your own machine. That runs on the standard streams as a subprocess with your own permissions, needs no authorization and no deployment, and takes an afternoon. Building this instead means paying for tenancy, tokens and operations to solve a problem you do not have.

items.title: MCP Server over stdio
items.description: An MCP server over stdio: exposing local tools, files and commands to a developer's own agent, with the process model and limits it implies.
items.use_when: Something on a developer's own machine should be available to their agent — a project's build system, an internal command-line tool, a local database, a scratch directory — and it runs as the same user with the same permissions they already have.
items.not_for: Anything reached over a network or used by more than one person. That is a different product: it needs authorization, tenant isolation, rate limits and a deployment, and none of those exist here — a stdio server has exactly the permissions of the process that spawned it, and that is the whole of its security model.

items.title: LLM Observability and Tracing
items.description: LLM observability and tracing: spans for model calls, prompt versions, token and cost attribution, and finding the run behind a bad answer.
items.use_when: A system that calls a model runs somewhere you cannot watch it, and someone will eventually say "it gave me a strange answer on Tuesday". Also when nobody can say which feature is responsible for the model bill.
items.not_for: Replacing your existing application observability. This is a layer on top of it — the same trace, with the model-specific fields that ordinary logging has no place for.

items.title: pgvector: Vector Search in Postgres
items.description: pgvector in PostgreSQL: index choice, HNSW tuning, filtered search and the post-filtering trap, without adding a second datastore to operate.
items.use_when: The data is already in Postgres, the corpus is large enough that a full scan is too slow, and you would rather have transactions, backups and joins than a second datastore to operate.
items.not_for: A corpus small enough to scan exhaustively — a few thousand vectors compare faster than an approximate index can be tuned, and an exact scan has perfect recall for free. Also not for search where the query is a product code, an error identifier or an exact phrase: embeddings are near-blind to those, and no amount of index tuning fixes it.

items.title: PostgreSQL Connection Pool and Lifecycle
items.description: A PostgreSQL connection layer: pool sizing, startup and shutdown, health checks and running behind a connection pooler in production.
items.use_when: A service needs Postgres and you want the connection lifecycle right before anything is built on top — pool sizing, startup, shutdown, health, and the pooler in front of it in production.
items.not_for: A short-lived script or a one-off job. A single connection opened and closed around the work is correct there, and a pool in a process that runs for four seconds is machinery with nothing to amortise. Also not the place to choose an ORM: this layer deliberately ends before that decision.

items.title: Prompt Structure and System Prompts
items.description: Prompt structure and system prompts: ordering for cache hits, rules that survive long contexts, and prompts that do not contradict themselves.
items.use_when: A prompt will run more than a handful of times — anything in a product path. Also when an existing prompt has grown by accretion and now contradicts itself, ignores rules, or caches badly.
items.not_for: One-off exploratory chat, or a prompt you will read once and throw away. Structure is cheap but it is not free of effort, and there is nothing here worth doing for a single run.

items.title: Pydantic Request and Response Schemas
items.description: Pydantic request and response schemas for FastAPI: separating what you accept from what you expose, with validation and safe response models.
items.use_when: An HTTP API accepts JSON bodies or returns objects built from database rows, and you want the accepted shape and the exposed shape to be two decisions rather than one accident.
items.not_for: An internal function boundary inside one process — types and a dataclass are enough there, and a validation layer between your own modules is cost with no attacker on the other side. Also not for the configuration your app reads at startup: that is validated once at boot, not per request, and the two get conflated constantly.

items.title: Pydantic Settings: Typed Configuration
items.description: Pydantic Settings for typed configuration: environment variables validated at startup, so a missing key is a failed deploy, not a 3am surprise.
items.use_when: Anything about how the app behaves comes from outside the code — a database URL, an API key, a feature flag, a timeout, a bucket name — and you want it wrong-or-missing to be a failed deploy rather than a runtime surprise.
items.not_for: Values that change while the process is running — feature flags flipped from a dashboard, per-tenant overrides, anything polled or pushed. Those are a runtime store with its own cache and invalidation, and freezing them into a settings object at startup is how a flag stops responding. Also not for validating user input; that arrives per request and belongs at the request boundary.

items.title: Qdrant Vector Search with Filters
items.description: Qdrant vector search with filters: collection design, payload indexing, filterable HNSW and quantisation for large filtered workloads.
items.use_when: The corpus is large, search is filtered by attributes on almost every query, and you want a store built for that rather than a general database extended to do it.
items.not_for: A corpus that comfortably fits in the database you already run. A second stateful service means a second backup story, a second upgrade path and a second thing to be woken up for, and below a few million vectors that cost usually buys nothing. Also not a source of truth: it holds derived data, and treating it as the only copy of anything is how a re-index becomes a data-loss incident.

items.title: Redis Cache Layer
items.description: A Redis cache layer: key design, TTLs, stampede protection, invalidation on write, and knowing what should happen when Redis is down.
items.use_when: A read is expensive and repeated — an aggregate over many rows, a third-party response, a permission set computed per request — and the answer is allowed to be slightly old.
items.not_for: Hiding a query that is slow because it is wrong. Caching an unindexed scan makes the first request slow and every later one fast, right up to the invalidation, and then the same scan runs under whatever load arrived meanwhile. Fix the query first; cache what is still expensive. Also not for data that must be exact on read — a balance, a stock level at checkout, a permission that has just been revoked.

items.title: Redis Rate Limiting and Job Queues
items.description: Redis rate limiting and job queues: sliding windows, atomic Lua counters, reliable queues, retries, dead letters and clean worker shutdown.
items.use_when: Requests must be bounded per caller, or work must happen outside the request — sending mail, generating a document, calling a slow third party — and losing that work is not acceptable.
items.not_for: Caching. It shares the server and nothing else: a cache may be lost entirely with no consequence, a queued job may not, and a design that treats them alike will lose jobs to an eviction policy. Also not for scheduled orchestration with dependencies between steps — that is a workflow engine, and building one on a queue is a project rather than a feature.

items.title: Async SQLAlchemy ORM Layer
items.description: An async SQLAlchemy ORM layer: a session per request, relationship loading without N+1, transactions and repositories you can test.
items.use_when: The data model has relationships worth traversing, several places need the same queries, and you want transaction boundaries in one place rather than repeated at every call site.
items.not_for: A service whose data access is a handful of hand-written analytical queries. An ORM adds an object graph, a session lifecycle and a loading strategy to a problem that had none, and for reporting workloads the SQL was the clearer artefact all along. Mixing is fine — the ORM for the write model, plain SQL for the reports.

items.title: Structured LLM Output with JSON Schema
items.description: Structured LLM output with JSON Schema: constrained decoding, validation, retries on malformed output and types that make constraints real.
items.use_when: The model's output feeds code rather than a person — extraction, classification, filling a form, producing arguments for something downstream — and a parse failure is an incident rather than a nuisance.
items.not_for: Prose a human will read. Forcing JSON onto a task that wants prose measurably degrades the prose, and you gain nothing your code can use.

items.title: Integration Tests with Real Dependencies
items.description: Integration tests with real dependencies: throwaway databases, containers, fixtures, isolation between tests and a suite that stays fast.
items.use_when: The interesting failures are in the seams — a query that is wrong, a constraint that fires, a migration that does not apply, a serialisation that differs from what the client expects — and a mocked dependency would have agreed with the code either way.
items.not_for: Logic that has no dependency. Running pure functions against a database container makes a ten-millisecond test a two-second one and proves nothing extra. Also not a replacement for production monitoring: these tests cover the inputs you thought of.

items.title: Test Harness and Unit Tests
items.description: A test harness and unit tests: project layout, fixtures, fakes over mocks, coverage that means something and tests that fail for one reason.
items.use_when: A project has no tests, or has tests that nobody trusts — they fail sometimes, they pass when the code is wrong, or they must be run in a particular order. Covers layout, fixtures, factories, mocking the outside world, and a coverage bar that is worth having.
items.not_for: Tests that need a real database, a real queue or a real HTTP peer. Those are integration tests: different infrastructure, different isolation problem, different speed budget. Trying to serve both from one harness is how a unit suite becomes a four-minute one nobody runs before pushing.

items.title: LLM Tool Design
items.description: LLM tool design: naming, parameters, descriptions and results a model can actually use, and the failures caused by tools that read badly.
items.use_when: An agent has more than one tool, and it picks the wrong one, sends malformed arguments, or misreads what came back. Also whenever tool schemas, descriptions or return shapes are being written or reworked.
items.not_for: A single-tool agent, or a call site where your code decides what runs and with which arguments. Nothing here applies when the model is not the one choosing.

items.title: LLM Tool Registry and Dispatcher
items.description: An LLM tool registry and dispatcher: declaring tools, validating arguments, result budgets, errors the model can act on and confirmation rules.
items.use_when: An agent has more than a handful of tools, they are added by more than one person, and the failures are now operational rather than descriptive — a schema that no longer matches its function, an argument that reached the code unchecked, one slow tool holding up the turn.
items.not_for: Designing an individual tool. What it should be called, how its description should read, what its arguments should be named and what shape its result should take are a different problem with a different answer, and doing it well matters more than anything here. Also not for a single-tool agent: a registry for one entry is indirection with no payoff.

items.title: Input Validation at the API Boundary
items.description: Input validation at the API boundary: parsing untrusted data once into types the rest of the code can trust, instead of checking everywhere.
items.use_when: Data arrives from anywhere you do not control — HTTP bodies, query strings, webhooks, queue messages, environment variables, third-party responses, model output — and the rest of the code should be able to trust it.
items.not_for: Validating your own database rows on the way out, or re-checking a value that has already been parsed once — that is duplicated logic that will drift.

items.title: FastAPI WebSocket Endpoint
items.description: A FastAPI WebSocket endpoint: connection lifecycle, authentication, heartbeats, backpressure and cleaning up when a client vanishes.
items.use_when: The server needs to push — live updates, a chat, a collaborative document, progress on a long job — and polling is either too slow or too expensive.
items.not_for: A stream that only flows from server to client, where server-sent events are simpler, survive proxies better and reconnect on their own. Also not for request-response dressed up as a socket: if every message expects exactly one reply, you have written HTTP with worse tooling and no caching. And not, on its own, for more than one replica — an in-process connection registry stops working at the second one.

items.title: WebSocket Broadcast with Redis Pub/Sub
items.description: WebSocket broadcast with Redis pub/sub: delivering messages across replicas, subscriber-loop health, delivery lag and duplicate handling.
items.use_when: A real-time feature already works on one process and now has to run on more than one — because it was scaled, or because a rolling deploy briefly runs two versions at once. That second case surprises people: you do not need to have chosen horizontal scaling to hit this.
items.not_for: A single-process deployment that will stay single-process, where an in-memory registry is correct and this is a service, a failure mode and a delivery guarantee you did not need. Also not a message queue: nothing here is durable, and using it for work that must not be lost is a category error §1 exists to prevent.

items.title: Mapping a repository
items.description: A skill that draws a codebase's architecture as a diagram: scan the repository, infer services, stores and boundaries, and render a map you can read.
